title: Staged Refactor: Check-in Heuristics and Quick Recovery Notes
content:
Purpose:
Short personal scratchpad for small, staged refactors (1–3 files / small service surface). Focus: safe check-ins, quick recovery, and signal triage. Not a formal runbook — quick notes to use during a fast rollout.

Context / principles (handy reminders):
- Prefer small, single-responsibility commits that are easy to revert.
- Each change should have a short smoke test that can be run locally and in canary.
- Assume that observability (traces/metrics/logs) will be the fastest way to detect regressions; add temporary tags/metrics if unsure.
- If unsure: reduce blast radius (smaller canary %, shorter TTL, feature flags).

Quick pre-checklist before pushing a staged refactor:
- [ ] linting passes (pre-commit hooks)
- [ ] unit tests for touched modules (run locally)
- [ ] relevant integration test(s) locally or in ephemeral environment
- [ ] add/verify a short smoke script (curl + expected substring)
- [ ] increment feature-flag key + default off in prod config
- [ ] add quick metric (counter) and trace tag around the changed path
- [ ] update PR description with rollout plan and rollback steps

Canary rollout heuristic (for ~low-risk changes):
1) Deploy to canary with flag OFF for traffic, run full smoke and integration check.
2) Flip flag to 2–5% traffic for 15m — watch for: 5xx count, p95 latency, error budget burn, increased database error rates.
3) If stable for 30m and no user-facing errors, widen to 20% for 30m.
4) Widen to 60% for 30m; if stable, promote to 100% during low-traffic window (or with on-call informed).
Notes: timelines can be compressed for low-risk config-only changes; extend for changes touching core request path.

Signals (primary + secondary):
- Primary: increase in 5xx (service), spike in p95 latency, error-rate on the specific route.
- Secondary: increase in DB connection errors, queue lag, cache miss rate, downstream 3rd-party latencies.
- Trace-level: missing expected spans, stack traces with new files/lines, unusual retry bursts.
- Side-channel: customer support queue mentions, automated end-to-end failures.

Quick triage flow if canary fails:
- Immediately flip flag OFF (if flag present). If not, revert canary deployment (git revert -> deploy).
- Confirm failure signature: is it broad 5xx or a narrow user-path?
- Collect: a) example failing request IDs, b) trace ids, c) logs from canary hosts (last 5 minutes), d) recent metric diffs.
- If root cause obvious and small -> patch + canary redeploy.
- If unknown -> roll back to previous revision and create incident note.
- Post-rollback: add a short follow-up TODO in PR: "why did canary fail?" and link the incident.

Fast local repro checklist (commands):
- git checkout -b staged-refactor/<short-desc>
- make test && ./scripts/smoke_local.sh (or: curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer localtoken" http://localhost:8080/route | grep "expected")
- docker-compose up --build (if service uses docker dev stack)
- TRACE_DEBUG=1 ./bin/server 2>&1 | tee local-trace.log

Rollback snippets (safe defaults):
- Revert commit: git revert <sha> --no-edit && git push origin HEAD
- If using infra deploy tool: redwoodctl deploy rollback --service <svc> --to <previous-rev>
- Quick config flip: curl -X POST https://flags.redwood.internal/toggle -d "flag=feature_x&state=off" (internal tooling)

Testing strategy notes (what to prioritize for small refactors):
- Unit tests: cover behaviour changes and edge cases. Fast.
- Integration tests: cover contract between modules touched, mock external deps.
- Smoke tests: string/substring checks; these should be fast and deterministic.
- E2E: expensive; only run on the widened canary or after promotion.

Observability hygiene to add while landing a refactor: (temporary additions OK)
- metric: "staged_refactor.<change>.requests" counter
- metric: "staged_refactor.<change>.errors" counter (sampled)
- span/tag: refactor_id=<pr-number> on entry span
- log: include refactor_id in DEBUG logs for a short TTL
Note: remove temporary metrics/tags once change is stable and follow up to clean up technical debt.

Open questions / TODOs (for follow-up before next refactor):
- TODO: standardize canary window length per service (SLO-based) — open ticket: JIRA-ENG-1985
- TODO: small script to auto-flip flag if error rate > threshold during canary (safety automation)
- Investigate why older canaries showed low p95 variance but user complaints still happened (likely client-side mismatch).

Post-merge follow-ups (to put into PR or personal issue):
- Add a one-line justification in deployment changelog: what was changed and why minimal risk.
- Schedule a 15m async post-mortem if canary had a notable blip (link traces + timeline).
- If we added temporary metrics / flags, add a TODO to remove cleanup after 2 weeks.

Notes to self (short shorthand):
- When in doubt, smaller = safer.
- Keep rollback path as simple as possible (flip flags before revert code).
- Make sure on-call knows the canary window + notification channel.

Examples of past quick wins (reminders):
- Replaced sync call with fast cached lookup in auth path -> landed with 5% canary, no regression, removed temp metric after 10d.
- Moved heavy init behind lazy load -> initial canary flagged an increase in cold starts; reduced canary duration and fixed by warming hook.

End of scratchpad.

(If this is useful, will formalize into a short team checklist under eng-serving-runtime/canary-playbook.)
